LA VIE EN ROUGE. France has its share of problems at the moment, from civil unrest over a widening gap in living standards to the broader planetary threat of climate change. The country just experienced its hottest summer on record, and now, three recent studies outline how global warming is a major risk to historic French heritage buildings going forward, reports Le Monde . There is the Château d’Azay-le-Rideau on an island in the Loire Valley, plagued by flooding, as well as the opposite—receding water levels that expose its wooden, foundational beams to air and decomposition. Among the three studies published since September is one by the Climate Institute at the Edhec Business School , which estimates that by 2050, 60 percent of listed French heritage sites will be in danger. Other studies include one by the publicly run Monuments Nationaux organization, and the Réseau Action Climat . Grégory Quenet , a professor who led the latter study, asks: “Are we ready to accept that floods will damage the Château de Chambord, that paintings will disappear at Lascaux [the cave], that the Strasbourg Cathedral will crumble…?”

BORN TO BE BOLD . New York’s New Museum director, Massimiliano Gioni, discusses the big challenges facing American museums today and where he wants to take the newly expanded institution, in an interview with Le Journal des Arts . With his new promotion from his former position as artistic director to the institution’s head honcho, Gioni said money had now become “a much greater preoccupation.” But he isn’t letting that get in the way of ambitious programming. “What matters is impact,” he said. “Our budget is increasing by about $8 million, but we remain at a scale that allows for risk-taking.” After all, “a certain radicalism” is in the museum’s DNA, he added. He also commented on the democratic responsibility of museums: “The fact that Donald Trump is attacking the Smithsonian is further proof: why does he spend so much time on the Smithsonian or the Kennedy Center ? Because he knows they embody values that many of us believe should be universal rather than determined by parties,” said Gioni.

TACITA MEETS MARISA. Tacita Dean discusses her new film about Arte Povera artist Marisa Merz with Financial Times reporter Caroline Roux, on the occasion of three institutional exhibitions celebrating the Italian artist, 100 years after her birth. Dean met Merz in 2005, when she was given a swift tour of her home and studio, which have been preserved as a museum. “She was incredibly … secretive,” remembers Dean of the late artist. “She barely let me see anything. It wasn’t exactly welcoming.” These days, “the onus is on us, the artists, to get out there, to do the marketing. We have to co-operate. They didn’t,” she said of Marisa Merz and her husband, fellow artist Mario Merz , who until recently enjoyed most of the critical acclaim. But even for his famous igloos and other installations, Marisa “worked on so many of his projects with him that they were mostly collaborations,” says Dean.
